item.title: Distance, Displacement, and Speed of a Hallway Robot
item.stimulus:
A delivery robot moves along a straight east–west hallway. Take east as the positive direction. Starting from its charging station, the robot makes three trips in order. During each trip it moves in only one direction.

Trip | Direction | Distance moved (m)
1 | east | 12
2 | west | 20
3 | east | 5

A second robot, Robot B, starts at the same charging station and makes a single trip of 3 m west.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance traveled by the first robot during the three trips. Then calculate its displacement from the charging station at the end of trip 3, giving it as a signed value and stating its direction.

criteria.text: Total distance = 12 m + 20 m + 5 m = 37 m, found by adding the sizes of the three trips without regard to direction.
criteria.evidence: Response adds the three trip lengths as positive quantities and gets 37 m.
criteria.fix: Distance is a scalar: add the length of every trip as a positive number, ignoring direction.

criteria.text: Displacement = (+12 m) + (−20 m) + (+5 m) = −3 m, that is, 3 m west of the charging station.
criteria.evidence: Response gives east trips positive signs and the west trip a negative sign, sums them to −3 m, and states the direction is west.
criteria.fix: Displacement is a vector: give each trip a sign for its direction, add the signed values, then read direction from the sign.

parts.prompt: Explain why the first robot's displacement at the end of trip 3 is equal to Robot B's displacement, even though the first robot traveled a much greater distance.

criteria.text: Explains that displacement is a vector sum in which trips in opposite directions have opposite signs and partly cancel, so the first robot's net change in position, −3 m, equals Robot B's −3 m; distance is a scalar, so nothing cancels.
criteria.evidence: Response states both displacements are −3 m (3 m west) and explains that the westward −20 m cancels most of the eastward +17 m in the vector sum, while distance only adds.
criteria.fix: When comparing displacements, add signed values so opposite trips cancel; only the net change in position from start to finish matters.

parts.prompt: During trip 2, the robot's velocity component is v_x = −0.80 m/s. A student states that the robot's speed during trip 2 is −0.80 m/s. Explain what is wrong with the student's statement, and give the robot's correct speed during trip 2.

criteria.text: States that the speed is 0.80 m/s, because speed is a scalar equal to the magnitude of the velocity and is never negative.
criteria.evidence: Response gives the speed as 0.80 m/s (positive) and identifies speed as a scalar or as the magnitude of velocity.
criteria.fix: Speed is a scalar: report the size of the velocity only, as a positive number, and drop the sign.

criteria.text: Explains that the negative sign in v_x = −0.80 m/s is direction information: the velocity, a vector, points west (the negative direction).
criteria.evidence: Response states that the minus sign shows the velocity is directed west, opposite to the chosen positive direction, and that speed does not carry direction.
criteria.fix: In one dimension, read the sign of a vector component as its direction; negative here means west.

item.model_answer:
(a) Total distance = 12 m + 20 m + 5 m = 37 m. Distance is a scalar, so each trip adds its length regardless of direction.
Displacement = (+12 m) + (−20 m) + (+5 m) = −3 m. The first robot ends 3 m west of the charging station.

(b) Displacement is a vector, so in the sum the eastward trips (+12 m and +5 m, total +17 m) and the westward trip (−20 m) have opposite signs and mostly cancel, leaving a net change in position of −3 m. Robot B's single trip also gives a displacement of −3 m, so the two displacements are equal (3 m west). Distance is a scalar, so for the first robot nothing cancels and it is 37 m, compared with 3 m for Robot B.

(c) Speed is a scalar equal to the magnitude of the velocity, so it cannot be negative. The robot's speed during trip 2 is 0.80 m/s. The negative sign in v_x = −0.80 m/s tells the direction of the velocity vector: the robot is moving west, the negative direction.

item.title: Center of Mass of a Loaded Rectangular Frame
item.stimulus:
Four small objects are fixed to the corners of a light, rigid rectangular frame of negligible mass. The frame lies flat in a horizontal plane. Positions are measured from corner A, with the x-axis along the 0.60 m side and the y-axis along the 0.40 m side. Treat each object as a particle.

Corner | x (m) | y (m)
A | 0 | 0
B | 0.60 | 0
C | 0.60 | 0.40
D | 0 | 0.40

Arrangement 1: a 1.0 kg object is fixed at each of the four corners.
Arrangement 2: the object at corner C is replaced by a 5.0 kg object; corners A, B, and D still hold 1.0 kg objects.

parts.prompt: Without using the center-of-mass equation, determine the location (x, y) of the center of mass of Arrangement 1. Justify your answer.

criteria.text: Locates the center of mass at (0.30 m, 0.20 m), justified because the four equal masses form a symmetric distribution, so the center of mass lies on both lines of symmetry, x = 0.30 m and y = 0.20 m, at their intersection.
criteria.evidence: Response gives (0.30 m, 0.20 m), the center of the rectangle, and justifies it with symmetry of the equal masses (the center of mass lies on the lines of symmetry).
criteria.fix: For equal masses placed symmetrically, find the lines of symmetry; the center of mass lies on each one, so it is where they cross.

parts.prompt: Calculate the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate of the center of mass of Arrangement 2.

criteria.evidence: Response uses x_cm = Σm·x/Σm with total mass 8.0 kg and obtains 0.45 m.
criteria.fix: Multiply each mass by its x-coordinate, add the products, then divide by the total mass of all four objects.

criteria.evidence: Response uses y_cm = Σm·y/Σm with total mass 8.0 kg and obtains 0.30 m.
criteria.fix: Repeat the weighted average for y separately; objects on the x-axis contribute zero to the sum but still count in total mass.

parts.prompt: The loaded frame in Arrangement 2 slides across a frictionless horizontal table without rotating. A student wants to describe how the frame moves as a whole without tracking the four objects separately. Describe how the student can model the system, including the mass of the model object and where it is located.

criteria.text: Models the frame and its four objects as a single object (particle) of mass 8.0 kg located at the system's center of mass, (0.45 m, 0.30 m).
criteria.evidence: Response states the system can be treated as one object (particle) with the total mass 8.0 kg, placed at the system's center of mass (the location found in the previous part, including a consistent follow-through value).
criteria.fix: To describe a system's overall motion, replace it with one object carrying the total mass and place it at the center of mass.

item.model_answer:
(a) The four objects have equal masses and sit at the corners of a rectangle, so the mass distribution is symmetric about the line x = 0.30 m and about the line y = 0.20 m. The center of mass lies on every line of symmetry, so it is at their intersection: (0.30 m, 0.20 m), the center of the rectangle.

(b) Total mass = 1.0 + 1.0 + 5.0 + 1.0 = 8.0 kg.
x_cm = (1.0·0 + 1.0·0.60 + 5.0·0.60 + 1.0·0)/8.0 = 3.6/8.0 = 0.45 m.
y_cm = (1.0·0 + 1.0·0 + 5.0·0.40 + 1.0·0.40)/8.0 = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30 m.
The center of mass is at (0.45 m, 0.30 m), shifted toward the heavy object at corner C.

(c) The four objects are rigidly attached and move together, so their individual properties do not matter for the motion of the whole system. The student can model the system as a single object of mass 8.0 kg located at the system's center of mass, (0.45 m, 0.30 m), and describe the motion of that one object.

item.title: Identifying the Forces on a Box Sliding Down a Ramp
item.stimulus: A box slides down a rough, straight ramp that makes an angle of 25° with the horizontal. The box speeds up as it slides. The ramp is fixed to the ground, air resistance is negligible, and nothing touches the box except the ramp.

parts.prompt: List every force exerted on the box while it slides. For each force, name the object that exerts it and describe its direction in words. Do not resolve the forces into components.

criteria.text: Gravitational force exerted by Earth on the box, directed vertically downward.
criteria.evidence: Response lists the gravitational force (weight, F_g, or mg), names Earth as the object exerting it, and gives its direction as straight down, not perpendicular to the ramp.
criteria.fix: Name Earth as the source of the gravitational force and point it straight down, whatever the tilt of the surface.
accepted_variants: weight exerted by Earth, straight down

criteria.text: Normal force exerted by the ramp on the box, directed perpendicular to the ramp surface and away from it.
criteria.evidence: Response lists the normal force, names the ramp as the object exerting it, and gives its direction as perpendicular to the ramp surface, away from the surface.
criteria.fix: A surface pushes perpendicular to itself: point the normal force at a right angle to the ramp, away from it, not straight up.

criteria.text: Friction force exerted by the ramp on the box, directed parallel to the ramp surface and up the ramp, opposite to the box's motion.
criteria.evidence: Response lists a friction force, names the ramp as the object exerting it, and gives its direction as along the ramp surface, up the ramp.
criteria.fix: On a rough surface add friction from that surface, directed along the surface opposite to the object's sliding motion.

parts.prompt: A classmate's list of forces on the box also includes "the force of the box's motion," directed down the ramp. Explain why this force should not be included.

criteria.text: Explains that every force is an interaction between the box and another object, and no object exerts a "force of motion" on the box; motion results from the forces exerted on the box and is not itself a force.
criteria.evidence: Response states that no other object exerts this force (an object cannot exert a force on itself), so it is not an interaction and does not belong on the list.
criteria.fix: Before listing a force, name the other object that exerts it; if no object can be named, it is not a force.

parts.prompt: To write equations for the box, a student chooses one coordinate axis parallel to the ramp surface and the other perpendicular to it. Explain one reason this choice of axes simplifies the analysis.

criteria.text: Gives a valid reason: the box accelerates along the ramp, so with an axis parallel to the ramp the acceleration lies entirely along one axis and its perpendicular component is zero; or, the normal and friction forces already lie along the chosen axes, so only the gravitational force must be split into components.
criteria.evidence: Response states either that the acceleration is parallel to the ramp and so has a component along only one axis, or that only the gravitational force is not along an axis.
criteria.fix: Choose one axis along the direction of acceleration; then the acceleration has a single nonzero component and the other axis has zero acceleration.

item.model_answer:
(a) Three forces are exerted on the box:
1. The gravitational force exerted by Earth, directed vertically downward.
2. The normal force exerted by the ramp, directed perpendicular to the ramp surface, away from the ramp.
3. The kinetic friction force exerted by the ramp, directed parallel to the ramp surface, up the ramp (opposite to the box's motion down the ramp).

(b) A force is always an interaction between the box and another object. No object exerts a "force of the box's motion" on the box, and an object cannot exert a force on itself. The box's motion down the ramp is the result of the forces listed above, not an additional force, so it should not be included.

(c) The box slides along the ramp, so its acceleration is parallel to the ramp surface. With one axis parallel to the ramp, the acceleration lies entirely along that axis and its component perpendicular to the ramp is zero. Also, the normal force and the friction force already lie along the two axes, so only the gravitational force has to be split into components.

item.title: Paired Forces Between a Tow Truck, a Cable, and a Car
item.stimulus: A tow truck pulls a car east along a straight, level road using a horizontal cable. The truck is east of the car. Treat the cable as ideal: its mass is negligible and it does not stretch. At one instant, the cable exerts a force of 1500 N directed east on the car.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude and direction of the force that the car exerts on the cable at this instant. Justify your answer.

criteria.text: The car exerts a force of 1500 N directed west on the cable, by Newton's third law: the force of the car on the cable is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force of the cable on the car.
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1500 N, west, and justifies it with Newton's third law (paired forces equal in magnitude and opposite in direction).
criteria.fix: For a force of A on B, the third-law partner is B on A: same magnitude, opposite direction, exerted on the other object.

parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude and direction of the force that the cable exerts on the truck at this instant. Justify your answer using a property of the cable.

criteria.text: The cable exerts a force of 1500 N directed west on the truck, because the tension in an ideal cable is the same at all points, so it pulls on the truck with the same magnitude as on the car, directed along the cable toward the car (west).
criteria.evidence: Response gives 1500 N, west, and justifies the magnitude by stating that tension is the same throughout an ideal (massless) cable.
criteria.fix: In an ideal string or cable, tension is equal at every point; each end pulls on its attached object along the cable, toward the middle.

parts.prompt: A student says: "The car pulls back on the cable with a force equal in size and opposite in direction to the cable's pull on the car, so these two forces cancel and the car cannot speed up." Explain the error in the student's reasoning.

criteria.text: Explains that the two forces in a third-law pair are exerted on different objects (one on the car, one on the cable), so they cannot cancel; only forces exerted on the car itself combine to determine the car's motion.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the paired forces act on different objects and therefore do not add together or cancel in describing the car's motion.
criteria.fix: Check which object each force is exerted on; third-law partners are always on different objects, so never cancel them against each other.

parts.prompt: Consider the system made up of the truck, the cable, and the car. Explain whether the forces that the cable exerts on the truck and on the car can change the velocity of this system's center of mass.

criteria.text: They cannot: the cable's forces on the truck and car are interactions between objects inside the chosen system (internal forces), and internal forces do not influence the motion of the system's center of mass.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies the cable forces as internal to the truck–cable–car system and states that internal forces do not change the motion of the system's center of mass.
criteria.fix: First decide whether both interacting objects are inside the system; if so, the forces are internal and cannot change the center-of-mass motion.

item.model_answer:
(a) By Newton's third law, the force the car exerts on the cable is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force the cable exerts on the car: F(car on cable) = −F(cable on car). So the car exerts 1500 N directed west on the cable.

(b) The cable is ideal, so the tension is the same at all points along it. The cable pulls on each attached object along the cable toward the other object. It pulls the car east with 1500 N, so it pulls the truck with 1500 N directed west, toward the car.

(c) The two forces the student describes form a third-law pair, and they are exerted on different objects: one is exerted on the car and the other on the cable. Forces exerted on different objects cannot cancel each other. Only forces exerted on the car itself determine whether the car speeds up, so the student's conclusion does not follow.

(d) No. The cable, truck, and car are all inside the chosen system, so the forces the cable exerts on the truck and on the car are internal forces. Internal forces do not influence the motion of a system's center of mass, so they cannot change the velocity of the center of mass of the truck–cable–car system.

item.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces in Three Situations
item.stimulus:
Situation 1: A child pulls a sled across level snow with a rope. The rope is at 37° above the horizontal and the tension in the rope is 50 N. The sled moves east in a straight line at a constant speed of 1.5 m/s. The gravitational force exerted on the sled by Earth is 300 N. The snow exerts a normal force and a horizontal friction force on the sled. Use sin 37° = 0.60 and cos 37° = 0.80.

Situation 2: A hockey puck slides east at 3.0 m/s across frictionless, level ice. Starting at time t = 0, a steady wind exerts a constant horizontal force on the puck directed north. The vertical forces on the puck remain balanced.

Situation 3: A bus on a straight, level road is speeding up while moving east. A small block of ice is placed on the floor of the bus, and friction between the ice and the floor is negligible. A passenger in the bus sees the block slide toward the back of the bus, even though no horizontal force is exerted on the block.

parts.prompt: For Situation 1, calculate the magnitude of the friction force and the magnitude of the normal force that the snow exerts on the sled.

criteria.text: Friction force magnitude = 50 N × cos 37° = 50 × 0.80 = 40 N, because the sled's velocity is constant, so the net force is zero and the horizontal forces balance.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the horizontal net force to zero (constant velocity) and finds friction = 40 N from the rope's horizontal component.
criteria.fix: Constant velocity means zero net force; balance the rope's horizontal component, T cos θ, against friction.

criteria.text: Normal force magnitude = 300 N − 50 N × sin 37° = 300 − 30 = 270 N, from balancing the vertical forces.
criteria.evidence: Response sets the vertical net force to zero, including the rope's upward component of 30 N, and finds the normal force = 270 N.
criteria.fix: Include the rope's upward component when balancing vertical forces; the normal force equals 300 N minus T sin θ, not 300 N.

parts.prompt: For Situation 2, describe what happens after t = 0 to the east component and to the north component of the puck's velocity. Justify your answer.

criteria.text: The east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s, because there is no east–west force on the puck, so the forces are balanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the east component remains 3.0 m/s (unchanged) and justifies it with zero net force in the east–west direction.
criteria.fix: Treat each direction separately: if forces along a direction are balanced, the velocity component along that direction stays constant.

criteria.text: The north component of velocity changes, increasing from zero in the northward direction, because the wind's force makes the net force northward, unbalanced in that direction.
criteria.evidence: Response states the north component of velocity changes (grows from zero, directed north) and justifies it with the unbalanced northward force.
criteria.fix: Velocity changes only in the direction of the unbalanced force; identify that direction and state that component changes.

parts.prompt: For Situation 3, is the bus an inertial reference frame? Justify your answer using Newton's first law.

criteria.text: No: in the bus's frame the ice block's velocity changes (it starts moving toward the back) even though the net force on it is zero, so an observer in the bus would not verify Newton's first law, and the bus is not an inertial frame.
criteria.evidence: Response says the bus is not inertial and justifies it by noting the block accelerates relative to the bus while the net force on it is zero, contradicting Newton's first law.
criteria.fix: Test a frame by asking whether objects with zero net force keep constant velocity there; if not, the frame is noninertial.

item.model_answer:
(a) The sled moves at constant velocity, so by Newton's first law the net force on it is zero.
Horizontal: the rope's horizontal component is 50 N × 0.80 = 40 N east, so the friction force has magnitude 40 N (directed west).
Vertical: the rope's vertical component is 50 N × 0.60 = 30 N up. F_N + 30 N − 300 N = 0, so the normal force has magnitude 270 N.

(b) After t = 0 there is still no force on the puck in the east–west direction, so the forces in that direction are balanced and the east component of velocity stays constant at 3.0 m/s. The wind's force makes the net force point north, so the forces are unbalanced in that direction and the north component of velocity changes: it increases from zero, directed north.

(c) No. The net force on the ice block is zero: the vertical forces balance and no horizontal force is exerted on it. Yet an observer in the bus sees the block's velocity change as it starts sliding toward the back. Newton's first law says an object with zero net force keeps a constant velocity, so this observer would not verify the first law. The speeding-up bus is therefore not an inertial reference frame.

item.title: Weight and Apparent Weight on a Larger Planet
item.stimulus: Planet P has twice the mass of Earth and twice the radius of Earth. Treat both planets as spheres with symmetrically distributed mass, and ignore their rotation. At Earth's surface the gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg. Ignore gravitational forces from all objects other than the planet being discussed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Planet P.

criteria.evidence: Response applies g = GM/r² with doubled mass and doubled radius and obtains 5.0 N/kg (or 5.0 m/s²).
criteria.fix: Write g = GM/r², replace M and r by their multiples, and simplify: doubling r divides g by four.

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut when the astronaut stands on its surface.

criteria.evidence: Response multiplies the astronaut's 60 kg mass by the surface field strength of Planet P to obtain 300 N (a consistent follow-through value from the previous part also earns this point).
criteria.fix: Weight is mass times the local field strength; use the field strength for Planet P, not Earth's 10 N/kg.

parts.prompt: The astronaut later travels in a spacecraft to a point that is a distance 3R from the center of Planet P, where R is the radius of Planet P. Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted by Planet P on the astronaut at that point.

criteria.text: The distance from the center triples, so F_g falls by a factor of 3² = 9: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.
criteria.evidence: Response uses the inverse-square dependence on distance from the planet's center (3R, not 2R) and obtains about 33 N (100/3 N).
criteria.fix: Measure r from the planet's center; with F ∝ 1/r², tripling r divides the force by nine.

parts.prompt: Back on the surface of Planet P, the astronaut stands on a scale in an elevator that has an upward acceleration of magnitude 2.0 m/s². Calculate the astronaut's apparent weight.

criteria.text: Apparent weight = normal force: F_N − mg_P = ma, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = 60(5.0 + 2.0) = 420 N.
criteria.evidence: Response identifies apparent weight as the normal (scale) force and obtains 420 N from F_N − mg = ma with upward acceleration.
criteria.fix: Apparent weight is the normal force; apply net force = ma with the acceleration's direction, so F_N exceeds mg when accelerating upward.

item.model_answer:
(a) The field strength at a planet's surface is g = GM/R². For Planet P, g_P = G(2M)/(2R)² = (2/4)(GM/R²) = (1/2)(10 N/kg) = 5.0 N/kg.

(b) F_g = m·g_P = (60 kg)(5.0 N/kg) = 300 N.

(c) The gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between centers. On the surface the distance is R; at the new point it is 3R, three times larger, so the force is 1/9 as large: F = 300 N/9 ≈ 33 N.

(d) The apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the scale. Taking up as positive, F_N − m·g_P = m·a, so F_N = m(g_P + a) = (60 kg)(5.0 m/s² + 2.0 m/s²) = 420 N. The apparent weight is 420 N, greater than the 300 N gravitational force because the astronaut accelerates upward.

item.title: Kinetic Energy of a Car Measured by Different Observers
item.stimulus: A car of mass 1200 kg travels east along a straight, level road at 15 m/s, as measured by an observer standing beside the road. Take east as the positive direction.

parts.prompt: Calculate the car's translational kinetic energy as measured by the roadside observer.

criteria.evidence: Response substitutes m = 1200 kg and v = 15 m/s into K = (1/2)mv² and obtains 135,000 J.
criteria.fix: Square the speed before multiplying: K = (1/2)mv², with v² = 225 m²/s² here.

parts.prompt: A truck with twice the mass of the car travels at half the car's speed, as measured by the roadside observer. Determine the ratio of the truck's kinetic energy to the car's kinetic energy.

criteria.evidence: Response shows that doubling the mass doubles K while halving the speed divides K by 4, giving a ratio of 1/2.
criteria.fix: Use K ∝ mv²: multiply the mass factor by the square of the speed factor.

parts.prompt: A second car, identical to the first, travels west at 15 m/s. A student says this car has negative kinetic energy because its velocity is negative. Explain whether the student is correct.

criteria.text: The student is incorrect: kinetic energy is a scalar that depends on v², which is positive for either direction, so the westbound car's kinetic energy is also +135,000 J.
criteria.evidence: Response states the student is wrong because kinetic energy is a scalar (no direction) and squaring the velocity removes the sign, so the second car has the same 135,000 J.
criteria.fix: Remember kinetic energy is a scalar: squaring velocity gives a positive value, so direction never affects K.

parts.prompt: An observer riding in a van that moves west at 5.0 m/s, as measured by the roadside observer, measures the motion of the first car. Calculate the first car's translational kinetic energy as measured by the observer in the van.

criteria.text: Car's velocity relative to the van = (+15 m/s) − (−5.0 m/s) = +20 m/s, so K = (1/2)(1200 kg)(20 m/s)² = 240,000 J.
criteria.evidence: Response finds the car's speed relative to the van as 20 m/s and obtains 240,000 J, recognizing that kinetic energy depends on the observer's reference frame.
criteria.fix: Find the object's velocity relative to the observer first (subtract the observer's signed velocity), then compute K with that speed.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percent decrease in the amount of Q present at 30 minutes in Extract 2 compared with Extract 1.

criteria.text: Calculates a percent decrease of 87.5%: (12.0 − 1.5) ÷ 12.0 × 100 = 87.5%.

item.title: Charge Compatibility at an Enzyme's Active Site
item.stimulus:
An enzyme catalyzes the breakdown of substrate S. The part of S that binds to the enzyme carries a negative charge, and the enzyme's active site contains amino acids with positively charged R groups. Researchers measured the initial rate of product formation in four tubes kept at the same temperature and pH.

Tube | Contents | Initial rate of product formation (μmol/min)
1 | Substrate S + normal enzyme | 48
2 | Substrate S + mutant enzyme | 2
3 | Substrate S, no enzyme | 0.5
4 | Substrate S′ + normal enzyme | 4

In the mutant enzyme, one positively charged R group in the active site is replaced by a negatively charged R group; the overall shape of the active site is unchanged. Substrate S′ has the same shape as substrate S but carries no charge.

parts.prompt: Calculate how many times faster product forms in tube 1 than in tube 3.

criteria.text: Calculates 48 ÷ 0.5 = 96, so product forms 96 times faster in tube 1.
criteria.evidence: Response divides the tube 1 rate by the tube 3 rate and obtains 96.
criteria.fix: To find how many times faster, divide the larger rate by the smaller rate; do not subtract.

parts.prompt: Explain how the normal enzyme causes the rate of product formation in tube 1 to be much higher than in tube 3.

criteria.text: Explains that the enzyme is a biological catalyst that lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so the reaction proceeds much faster than without the enzyme.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the enzyme lowers the activation energy (energy needed to start the reaction), which increases the reaction rate.
criteria.fix: When explaining an enzyme's effect on rate, name activation energy and state that the enzyme lowers it.

parts.prompt: Explain why the mutant enzyme in tube 2 has much lower activity than the normal enzyme.

criteria.text: Explains that the substituted negatively charged R group makes the charge of the active site incompatible with the negatively charged substrate S (like charges repel), so S binds poorly and few enzyme–substrate complexes form.
criteria.evidence: Response links the new negative charge in the active site to loss of charge compatibility with negative S and to reduced substrate binding or reduced enzyme–substrate complex formation.
criteria.fix: Compare the charges of active site and substrate; opposite charges attract, while like charges repel and prevent the enzyme–substrate complex.

parts.prompt: The normal enzyme acts slowly on substrate S′ even though S′ has the same shape as S. Explain why.

criteria.text: Explains that for the reaction to occur, both the shape and the charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site; S′ fits the shape but lacks the negative charge attracted by the positive R groups, so it binds poorly and forms few enzyme–substrate complexes.
criteria.evidence: Response states that charge, not only shape, must match the active site and that uncharged S′ is not attracted to the positively charged R groups, so binding is reduced.
criteria.fix: Remember the enzyme–substrate model requires compatible shape and charge; check both properties for any substrate.

item.model_answer:
(a) 48 μmol/min ÷ 0.5 μmol/min = 96. Product forms 96 times faster in tube 1 than in tube 3.

(b) The enzyme is a biological catalyst. It lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so far more substrate molecules can react per minute than in tube 3, where the reaction occurs without the enzyme.

(c) Substrate S binds through a negatively charged region, which is attracted to the positively charged R groups in the normal active site. In the mutant, a negatively charged R group replaces a positive one, so the active site's charge is no longer compatible with S; the like charges repel. S therefore binds poorly, few enzyme–substrate complexes form, and the rate drops to 2 μmol/min.

(d) For an enzyme-mediated reaction to occur, both the shape and the charge of the substrate must be compatible with the active site. S′ has the right shape but no charge, so it is not attracted to the positively charged R groups in the active site. S′ binds poorly, few enzyme–substrate complexes form, and the rate is only 4 μmol/min.

item.title: A Sequential Pathway and Energy Coupling in a Bacterium
item.stimulus:
A bacterium makes molecule D from molecule A through a three-step pathway. Each step is catalyzed by a different enzyme.

Step 1: A → B
Step 2: B → C
Step 3: C → D

Researchers measured the concentrations of the pathway molecules in normal cells and in a mutant strain that lacks a working enzyme for one of the three steps.

Molecule | Normal cells (mM) | Mutant cells (mM)
A | 1.0 | 1.1
B | 0.4 | 6.5
C | 0.3 | 0.0
D | 2.0 | 0.0

Step 3 requires an input of energy. In the cell, step 3 is coupled to reaction E, which releases energy. Reaction E releases 30 kJ of energy per mole, and step 3 requires 21 kJ of energy per mole.

parts.prompt: Using the data, identify the step that is blocked in the mutant strain.

criteria.text: Identifies step 2 (B → C) as the blocked step.
criteria.evidence: Response names step 2 (B → C).
criteria.fix: Find where a pathway molecule piles up and the next molecule is missing; the blocked step lies between them.

parts.prompt: The enzyme for step 3 works normally in the mutant cells. Explain why the mutant cells contain no D.

criteria.text: Explains that in a sequential pathway the product of one step is the reactant for the next step: C, the product of step 2, is the reactant for step 3, so with no C made, step 3 cannot produce D.
criteria.evidence: Response states that step 3 needs C as its reactant and that C is not made because step 2 is blocked, so no D is formed.
criteria.fix: Trace the pathway forward: each step's product feeds the next step, so a missing reactant stops every later step.

parts.prompt: Explain how coupling step 3 to reaction E allows step 3 to occur in the cell.

criteria.text: Explains that the energy released by reaction E is used to supply the energy that step 3 requires; because E releases more energy (30 kJ per mole) than step 3 needs (21 kJ per mole), the coupled processes can proceed together.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the energy-releasing reaction E provides the energy input required by the energy-requiring step 3, and notes that E releases at least as much energy as step 3 needs.
criteria.fix: Describe coupling as an energy-releasing process paying for an energy-requiring one, and check that energy released exceeds energy required.

parts.prompt: Calculate the amount of energy per mole released by reaction E that is not used to drive step 3, and describe what happens to this energy.

criteria.text: Calculates 30 kJ − 21 kJ = 9 kJ per mole not used by step 3.
criteria.evidence: Response subtracts the energy required by step 3 from the energy released by E and obtains 9 kJ per mole.
criteria.fix: Subtract energy required from energy released; the difference is the energy left over from the coupled reactions.

criteria.text: Describes that the extra energy is released to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy); it is not destroyed, consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the unused energy is lost to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy), not destroyed or stored.
criteria.fix: Remember energy transfers are never complete: energy not captured is released as heat, and energy is never destroyed.

item.model_answer:
(a) Step 2 (B → C) is blocked. In the mutant, B builds up to 6.5 mM (compared with 0.4 mM in normal cells), while C is absent (0.0 mM). B is the reactant of step 2 and C is its product, so the block is at step 2.

(b) The pathway is sequential: the product of one step is the reactant for the next. C, the product of step 2, is the reactant for step 3. Because step 2 is blocked, no C is made, so even though the step 3 enzyme works, step 3 has no reactant and no D is produced.

(c) Step 3 requires an input of energy that it cannot supply itself. When step 3 is coupled to reaction E, the energy released by reaction E is used to provide the energy step 3 requires. Reaction E releases 30 kJ per mole, more than the 21 kJ per mole step 3 needs, so the coupled processes can proceed together.

(d) 30 kJ − 21 kJ = 9 kJ per mole is not used to drive step 3. This energy is released to the surroundings as heat (thermal energy). It is not destroyed, consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
